conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can show up any time in the first year postpartum, and it includes a question about self-harm. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no right or wrong answers, only what’s true for you. I’ll ask each question in everyday language, and we’ll go at your pace.

Let’s start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Hi Sarah. Honestly, most of the time I can still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but if my husband makes a joke or I see something silly on my phone, a little laugh still slips out. It’s just… not quite as strong or as often.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still get a chuckle out, but it feels kind of muted—like I have to remind myself it’s okay to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or cuddling the baby when she’s sleepy—but the excitement isn’t as big as it used to be. It’s more “that’ll be nice” than “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday she spit up a ton right after I fed her and I immediately thought, “I must have done something wrong—did I eat the wrong thing, hold her wrong?” I know it’s probably not rational, but the thought pops in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my mind just races—like I’ll lie down and suddenly worry that her breathing sounds different, or I’ll imagine she’s too warm even though the monitor says she’s fine. It’s not all day, but a couple of times this week it hit me out of nowhere and I had to take a few deep breaths to settle myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky, but there was one night I woke up suddenly and my heart was racing because I thought I’d slept through her cry. Turns out she hadn’t even stirred, but for a minute I felt shaky and had to sit up and sip some water before I could lie back down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when she won’t nap and the laundry is piled up, I feel this tightness in my chest and think, “How am I going to get through the rest of the day?” But if I take it one small task at a time, I usually manage.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I can fall asleep okay once the baby’s down, but sometimes my brain keeps replaying the day—did I burp her long enough, did I snap at my partner—and it takes me maybe 20–30 extra minutes to drift off. It’s more little worries than being really unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel a bit down a couple of days a week—like yesterday I just sat on the couch with her wrapped against me and felt this heavy, blah mood. It lifts when someone visits or when she smiles, but the sad cloud comes and goes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve teared up twice this week. Once was when she wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing her; the other time my mom left after dropping off food and I just felt suddenly alone. It wasn’t sobbing, more quiet tears that stopped after a minute or two.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or tearful, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 11: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Structured Note  
Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire; patient is 2–3 wks post-delivery.

I. Symptoms / Observable Concerns  
- Subjective low mood: endorses “sad or miserable” several days/week, transient improvement with social contact.  
- Anhedonia: describes enjoyment as “muted,” anticipatory pleasure reduced to “that’ll be nice.”  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: automatic thoughts of “I must have done something wrong” when routine infant events occur.  
- Worry / physiological anxiety: racing thoughts, sudden heart-rate increase, somatic concern about infant well-being; not meeting full panic frequency/intensity.  
- Overwhelm / coping strain: chest tightness when tasks accumulate; improves with stepwise approach.  
- Sleep-onset delay: 20–30 min due to rumination about daily parenting performance.  
- Crying spells: twice this week, linked to feeding difficulty and perceived social isolation.  
- Suicidality: denied, no self-harm thoughts endorsed.

II. Pattern Summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety features; functional impact present (sleep disruption, task-related distress) but no safety concerns at this time.

III. Screening Relevance  
Meets partial criteria for provisional consideration of minor-moderate postpartum depression and/or generalized anxiety; does not meet threshold for major depression or panic disorder on screening data alone. No red-flag safety items.

IV. Next Screening Considerations  
- Repeat EPDS at 2-week interval or sooner if worsening.  
- Evaluate social support, partner involvement, and practical help.  
- Provide psycho-education on normative vs. clinical ranges; discuss low-intensity interventions (peer support, structured sleep/feeding schedule, brief CBT or mindfulness).  
- Immediate re-contact advised for persistent sadness, functional decline, or emergence of self-harm ideation.
